claim: Pediatric neural tumors are often initiated during early development and can undergo very rapid transformation.
source: Pediatric neural tumors are often initiated during early development and can undergo very rapid transformation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The molecular basis of early malignant susceptibility in pediatric neural tumors remains unknown.
source: However, the molecular basis of this early malignant susceptibility remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: During Drosophila development, neural stem cells divide asymmetrically and generate intermediate progenitors that rapidly differentiate into neurons.
source: During Drosophila development, neural stem cells (NSCs) divide asymmetrically and generate intermediate progenitors that rapidly differentiate in neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila neural development.

claim: Upon gene inactivation, intermediate progenitors can dedifferentiate and generate malignant tumors.
source: Upon gene inactivation, these progeny can dedifferentiate and generate malignant tumors.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intermediate progenitors are prone to malignancy only when born during an early window of development while expressing Chinmo, Imp/IGF2BP, and Lin-28.
source: Here, we find that intermediate progenitors are prone to malignancy only when born during an early window of development while expressing the transcription factor Chinmo, and the mRNA-binding proteins Imp/IGF2BP and Lin-28.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2, 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Chinmo, Imp/IGF2BP, and Lin-28 compose an oncogenic module that is coopted upon dedifferentiation of early-born intermediate progenitors to drive unlimited tumor growth.
source: These genes compose an oncogenic module that is coopted upon dedifferentiation of early-born intermediate progenitors to drive unlimited tumor growth.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by data in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Temporal transcription factor progression in NSCs silences the oncogenic module, thereby limiting mitotic potential and terminating the window of malignant susceptibility.
source: In late larvae, temporal transcription factor progression in NSCs silences the module, thereby limiting mitotic potential and terminating the window of malignant susceptibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Many pediatric tumors are thought to initiate during prenatal stages and are able to rapidly progress towards malignancy, sometimes within a few months.
source: Many pediatric tumors are thought to initiate during prenatal stages and are able to rapidly progress towards malignancy, sometimes within a few months (Marshall et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Marshall et al., 2014.

claim: Pediatric tumors contain very few genetic alterations.
source: Yet, they contain very few genetic alterations (Huether et al., 2014; Parsons et al., 2011; Pugh et al., 2013; Vogelstein et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transformation in infancy is not driven by the gradual accumulation of genetic lesions over many years, as for most adult cancers.
source: suggesting that transformation in infancy is not driven by the gradual accumulation of genetic lesions over many years, as for most adult cancers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that pediatric tumors have few genetic alterations.

claim: Cells born during early development appear predisposed to malignant transformation.
source: Instead, cells born during early development appear predisposed to malignant transformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the characteristics of pediatric tumors.

claim: Drosophila is a well-established animal model to investigate basic principles of tumorigenesis in the developing or ageing organism.
source: Drosophila is a well-established animal model to investigate basic principles of tumorigenesis in the developing or ageing organism (Gonzalez, 2013; Siudeja et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Single gene inactivation perturbing the asymmetric divisions of neural stem cells during development can rapidly cause NB amplification and aggressive malignant tumors in transplantation assays.
source: In particular, it has been used to demonstrate that single gene inactivation perturbing the asymmetric divisions of neural stem cells (NSCs), called neuroblasts (NBs) in Drosophila, during development can rapidly cause NB amplification and aggressive malignant tumors in transplantation assays (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Knoblich, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of transformation in Drosophila neural tumors are still unknown.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms of transformation are still unknown (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Knoblich, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of a knowledge gap supported by citations.

claim: Normal NBs are active from embryogenesis to pupal stages and generate the neurons and glial cells that constitute the Drosophila central nervous system.
source: Normal NBs are active from embryogenesis to pupal stages and generate the neurons and glial cells that constitute the Drosophila central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Type-I NBs self-renew while giving rise to a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which usually divides once to generate two post-mitotic neurons or glia.
source: Upon asymmetric division, most NBs (type-I) self-renew while giving rise to an intermediate progenitor, called the ganglion mother cell (GMC), which usually divides once to generate two post-mitotic neurons or glia.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila neural development, supported by a citation.

claim: Type-II NBs generate intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) that can produce a few GMCs allowing for an amplification of post-mitotic progeny in the lineage.
source: In contrast, a small number of NBs (type-II) located in the central brain region of the CNS, generates intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) that can produce a few GMCs allowing for an amplification of post-mitotic progeny in the lineage (Homem and Knoblich, 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: NBs undergo a limited number of divisions during development and invariably stop dividing before adulthood.
source: NBs undergo a limited number of divisions during development and invariably stop dividing before adulthood (Truman and Bate, 1988).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: For NBs located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) of the CNS, limited mitotic potential is governed by a NB-intrinsic clock that schedules their terminal differentiation during metamorphosis.
source: For NBs located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) of the CNS, this limited mitotic potential is governed by a NB-intrinsic clock that schedules their terminal differentiation during metamorphosis (Maurange et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The timing mechanism in VNC NBs is set by the sequential expression of a series of 'temporal' transcription factors that has the ability to endow each progeny with a different neuronal identity according to their birth order.
source: This timing mechanism is set in NBs by the sequential expression of a series of 'temporal' transcription factors that has the ability to endow each progeny with a different neuronal identity according to their birth order (Kohwi and Doe, 2013; Maurange, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NBs in the VNC need to progress up to a late temporal factor in the series to become competent to respond to the hormonal cues promoting cell cycle exit and terminal differentiation during metamorphosis.
source: In addition, NBs in the VNC need to progress up to a late temporal factor in the series to become competent to respond to the hormonal cues promoting cell cycle exit and terminal differentiation during metamorphosis (Homem et al., 2014; Maurange et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In VNC NBs, there are four known temporal transcription factors (Hunchback (Hb) -> Kruppel (Kr) -> Pdm -> Castor (Cas)) mainly expressed during embryogenesis.
source: In VNC NBs, there are four known temporal transcription factors (Hunchback (Hb) -> Kruppel (Kr) -> Pdm -> Castor (Cas)) mainly expressed during embryogenesis (Baumgardt et al., 2009; Grosskortenhaus et al., 2005; Isshiki et al., 2001; Kambadur et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cas is re-expressed in early larval NBs presumably followed by other, yet unknown, temporal factors required to set up a late global transition of neuronal identity during larval development and to schedule NB termination during metamorphosis.
source: Cas is re-expressed in early larval NBs presumably followed by other, yet unknown, temporal factors required to set up a late global transition of neuronal identity during larval development and to schedule NB termination during metamorphosis (Maurange et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement combining established knowledge and speculation, supported by a citation.

claim: Progression throughout the temporal transcription factor sequence is governed by cross-regulatory transcriptional interactions between the temporal transcription factors.
source: Progression throughout the sequence is governed by cross-regulatory transcriptional interactions between the temporal transcription factors, and can be blocked by continuous mis-expression of a temporal factor or by its inactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Isshiki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Seven-up (Svp), an orphan nuclear receptor orthologous to mammalian COUP-TF transcription factors, can promote transitions between temporal transcription factors.
source: Transitions between temporal transcription factors can also be promoted by Seven-up (Svp), an orphan nuclear receptor orthologous to mammalian COUP-TF transcription factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Svp is transiently expressed in embryonic NBs to promote the early Hb->Kr transition, and in larval NBs to trigger a global temporal transition allowing NBs to switch from generating an early subpopulation of neurons expressing Chinmo to a later sub-population expressing other markers.
source: In particular, Svp is transiently expressed in embryonic NBs, to promote the early Hb->Kr transition, and in larval NBs to trigger a global temporal transition allowing NBs to switch from generating an early subpopulation of neurons expressing the BTB transcription factor Chinmo to a later sub-population expressing other markers (Benito-Sipos et al., 2011; Kanai et al., 2005; Maurange et al., 2008; Mettler et al., 2006).

claim: Inactivation of Svp during early larval stages blocks NBs in an early temporal identity.

claim: Late svp-/- NBs continuously generate Chinmo+ neurons, fail to undergo terminal differentiation during metamorphosis, and continue to divide in adults.
source: Consequently, late svp-/- NBs continuously generate Chinmo+ neurons, fail to undergo terminal differentiation during metamorphosis, and continue to divide in adults (Maurange et al., 2008).

claim: Multiple series of temporal transcription factors have been uncovered in the different regions of the CNS.
source: Multiple series of temporal transcription factors have been uncovered in the different regions of the CNS, and recent data suggests that this temporal patterning system is evolutionary conserved and operating in mammalian NSCs (Brand and Livesey, 2011; Konstantinides et al., 2015; Li et al., 2013; Mattar et al., 2015).
